commentary.seminaVerbi:
David’s lion-play is the archetype of trained ferocity: the psyche rehearses danger until it becomes intimate, the way a Zen swordsman or a Shaolin adept makes fear into a familiar tool. It is not innocence; it is aggression disciplined into protection. The “sweet melody” before the altar turns violence into order, like Orphic song taming the underworld or the Vedic idea that right chant stabilizes the world; speculation: art here is the sublimation that keeps power from rotting into mere appetite.

Herod is a study in weak will enthroned. He “fears” the just man and enjoys hearing him, yet lets his image at a banquet murder his conscience; this is Plato’s tyrant-soul, enslaved by desire and the gaze of others. The birthday feast becomes a Dionysian court where eros and spectacle write law, and the prophet’s severed head is the grisly anti-sacrament, closer to the scapegoat mechanism René Girard traces in many cultures. The oath functions like dharma misread as face-saving: a vow treated as fate, when it is only vanity hardened into destiny.
commentary.excursus:
Sirach polishes David into a usable myth: the boy who pets predators, the man who turns slaughter into song. But the music is not an afterthought; it is the technology that makes violence feel like vocation. “With his whole heart” he loves the maker who authorizes his appetite. The sweet melody is the seal over a mouth that has tasted blood.

Mark shows what happens when power loses the ability to sanctify itself. Herod is not a tyrant of conviction but of nerves. He “hears willingly” because John’s voice gives him the sensation of being judged, and that sensation feels like life. He keeps the prophet like a caged conscience, a dangerous pet.

Then desire enters as performance: a dance, a room of watching men, a vow spoken to preserve an image. The head on a dish is not simply cruelty; it is the banquet’s true course, the price of male bravado and female resentment, the conversion of speech into meat. David’s singers make killing sound holy; Herod’s guests make it look inevitable. In both, dread and desire collaborate to turn a human throat into an instrument—either for praise or for silence.
commentary.synthesis: God’s anointed power is ordered toward thanksgiving and worship; worldly power, ruled by appetite and audience, converts truth-telling into a trophy and calls it necessity.

gospel.text: The narrative dissects weak authority: Herod is governed by a triangle—illicit bond, domestic resentment, public spectators. He oscillates between fascination with the holy and fear of losing face, and the banquet seals the trap: an oath spoken for an audience becomes a law stronger than conscience. The disciples’ burial is the only coherent act left; it exposes the court’s spectacle as sterile power.

reading.text: The passage edits kingship into doxology: the public achievements are narrated as praise-acts, so rule is legitimated by attribution. The political arc bends toward cultic order; the king’s greatness is measured by whether glory is returned upward rather than hoarded.

marginalia.text: Election rendered as butchery: the chosen is what is cut away.
Predation domesticated; the shepherd’s child plays at Eden with teeth still present.
Tiny stone, huge mouth; boasting is a physical thing to be struck down.
Invocation precedes force; the “right hand” is lent, not owned.
Horn-language: power is treated as an animal growth that can be broken.
After blood, liturgy: violence resolves into ordered sound.
Guilt manufactures miracles: the dead must return to explain the living.
He names the deed plainly—“I beheaded”—and still calls it resurrection.
Law is a sentence, not advice; it makes the bedroom a courtroom.
“Convenient day”: time itself becomes an accomplice.
Half a kingdom offered to a dancer: sovereignty auctioned by impulse.
Haste plus “forthwith”: desire wants speed more than reasons.
The head circulates as a gift; murder converted into table-service.

hoursOfPrayer.prayer: O God, strength of all the saints, who have called Saint Paul Miki and his companions to eternal life through the cross: grant us, through their intercession, to hold fast with vigor, even unto death, the faith we profess. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, who lives and reigns with you in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, for ever and ever.
hoursOfPrayer.label: Matins

hoursOfPrayer.prayer: O God, strength of all the saints, who have called Saint Paul Miki and his companions to eternal life by way of the cross, grant us, through their intercession, to keep with steadfast courage, even unto death, the faith we profess. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, who lives and reigns with you in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God for ever and ever.
hoursOfPrayer.label: Lauds

hoursOfPrayer.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, who at the hour of Terce were led to the torment of the Cross for the salvation of the world, help us to weep over the sins of our past life and to avoid faults in the time to come. You who live and reign for ever and ever.
hoursOfPrayer.label: Terce

hoursOfPrayer.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, who at the hour of Sext mounted the cross for our salvation while darkness covered the world, grant that your light may always shine upon us, so that, guided by it, we may attain eternal life. You who live and reign for ever and ever.
hoursOfPrayer.label: Sext

hoursOfPrayer.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, who, hanging upon the cross, granted the repentant thief the eternal kingdom, look upon us, who, like him, confess our sins, and grant that we too, like him, may enter, after death, into paradise. You who live and reign for ever and ever.
hoursOfPrayer.label: Nones

hoursOfPrayer.prayer: O God, the strength of all the saints, who through the Cross have called Saint Paul Miki and his companions to eternal life, grant us, through their intercession, to hold fast with courage, even unto death, to the faith we profess. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, who lives and reigns with you in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, for ever and ever.
hoursOfPrayer.label: Vespers

hoursOfPrayer.prayer:
Let us pray:

Lord, almighty God: since by our rest we are going to imitate your Son, who rested in the tomb, we ask that, when we rise tomorrow, we may also imitate him by rising to a new life. Through Jesus Christ our Lord.
hoursOfPrayer.label: Compline

lines: And as the fat taken away from the flesh, so was David chosen from among the children of Israel.
He played with lions as with lambs: and with bears he did in like manner as with the lambs of the flock, in his youth.
Did not he kill the giant, and take away reproach from his people?
In lifting up his hand, with the stone in the sling he beat down the boasting of Goliath:
For he called upon the Lord the Almighty, and he gave strength in his right hand, to take away the mighty warrior, and to set up the horn of his nation.
So in ten thousand did he glorify him, and praised him in the blessings of the Lord, in offering to him a crown of glory:
For he destroyed the enemies on every side, and extirpated the Philistines the adversaries unto this day: he broke their horn for ever.
In all his works he gave thanks to the holy one, and to the most High, with words of glory.
With his whole heart he praised the Lord, and loved God that made him: and he gave him power against his enemies:
And he set singers before the altar, and by their voices he made sweet melody.

lines: And king Herod heard, (for his name was made manifest,) and he said: John the Baptist is risen again from dead, and therefore mighty works shew forth themselves in him.
And others said: It is Elias. But others said: It is a prophet, as one of the prophets.
Which Herod hearing, said: John whom I beheaded, he is risen again from the dead.
For Herod himself had sent and apprehended John, and bound him prison for the sake of Herodias the wife of Philip his brother, because he had married her.
For John said to Herod: It is not lawful for thee to have thy brother's wife.
Now Herodias laid snares for him: and was desirous to put him to death and could not.

For Herod feared John, knowing him to be a just and holy man: and kept him, and when he heard him, did many things: and he heard him willingly. And kept him... That is, from the designs of Herodias; and for fear of the people, would not put him to death, though she sought it; and through her daughter she effected her wish.
And when a convenient day was come, Herod made a supper for his birthday, for the princes, and tribunes, and chief men of Galilee.

And when the daughter of the same Herodias had come in, and had danced, and pleased Herod, and them that were at table with him, the king said to the damsel: Ask of me what thou wilt, and I will give it thee.
And he swore to her: Whatsoever thou shalt ask I will give thee, though it be the half of my kingdom.
Who when she was gone out, said to her mother, What shall I ask? But her mother said: The head of John the Baptist.
And when she was come in immediately with haste to the king, she asked, saying: I will that forthwith thou give me in a dish, the head of John the Baptist.
And the king was struck sad. Yet because of his oath, and because of them that were with him at table, he would not displease her:
But sending an executioner, he commanded that his head should be brought in a dish.
And he beheaded him in the prison, and brought his head in a dish: and gave to the damsel, and the damsel gave it her mother.
Which his disciples hearing came, and took his body, and laid it in a tomb.
